dominio: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources
spiegazione: Correct: c. A module is referenced by its symbolic name, and module outputs are read through the outputs property, so the expression is stgModule.outputs.storageEndpoint. Wrong: a. 'storageDeploy' is the value of the name property, which becomes the name of the nested deployment resource in the generated ARM template; it is not the symbolic name and cannot be used to reference the module in the Bicep file. Wrong: b. params holds the values passed INTO the module; it does not expose values returned by the module. Wrong: d. The reference() ARM function is not the Bicep idiom for module outputs; Bicep resolves module outputs through the symbolic name, and using reference() here does not compile against the module's name property.

dominio: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources
sotto_argomento: Deploy resources by using an Azure Resource Manager template or a Bicep file
domanda:
A resource group named RG1 contains a storage account named sa1. A colleague runs the following command:

az deployment group create --resource-group RG1 --template-file main.bicep

The main.bicep file defines a virtual network only. It does not reference sa1. What happens to sa1?
opzione_a: sa1 is deleted because it is not defined in main.bicep.
opzione_c: The deployment fails because RG1 contains a resource that is not in the template.
opzione_d: The properties of sa1 that are not specified in main.bicep are reset to their default values.
spiegazione: Correct: b. The default deployment mode is Incremental. In incremental mode, Resource Manager leaves unchanged the resources that exist in the resource group but are not specified in the template, and adds the resources that are in the template. Wrong: a. Deleting resources that are absent from the template is Complete mode behaviour, which must be requested explicitly with --mode Complete; it is not the default. Wrong: c. Extra resources in the resource group never cause a deployment failure in either mode. Wrong: d. Property reset to defaults does happen in incremental mode, but only when a resource IS redeployed by the template and the property is omitted from its definition. sa1 is not in the template at all, so it is not touched.

dominio: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources
sotto_argomento: Export a deployment as an Azure Resource Manager template or convert an Azure Resource Manager template to a Bicep file
domanda: Your team keeps a library of ARM JSON templates and has decided that all new authoring will be done in Bicep. You download a template named main.json and want to produce an equivalent Bicep file. Which Azure CLI command should you run?
spiegazione: Correct: a. az bicep decompile --file main.json converts an ARM JSON template to Bicep and creates main.bicep in the same directory as main.json. Use --force to overwrite an existing main.bicep. Wrong: b. az bicep build compiles in the opposite direction: it transpiles a .bicep file into an ARM JSON template. Wrong: c. az bicep build-params compiles a .bicepparam parameters file into a JSON parameters file; it does not convert a template. Wrong: d. There is no az deployment group export command that converts a local file; template export is performed with az group export against live resources, and the result is still JSON that you must then decompile.

dominio: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources
domanda:
A Bicep file that deploys a virtual machine declares the following parameter:

param adminPassword string

During a security review, an auditor finds that the value supplied for adminPassword is visible in the deployment history in the Azure portal. You must prevent the value from being logged or displayed, while making the smallest possible change to the file. What should you do?
opzione_a: Add the @description('Sensitive') decorator above the parameter declaration.
opzione_b: Add the @metadata({ secure: true }) decorator above the parameter declaration.
opzione_c: Add the @secure() decorator above the parameter declaration.
opzione_d: Change the parameter type from string to int and pass a hash of the password.
spiegazione: Correct: c. When a parameter is decorated with @secure(), Azure Resource Manager treats the value as sensitive: it is not saved to the deployment history and is not logged or displayed in the portal or in command-line output. @secure() is valid on parameters of type string and object, so it applies here. Wrong: a. @description() only supplies help text that is shown to users in the portal; it has no effect on how the value is stored or logged. Wrong: b. @metadata() attaches arbitrary custom properties for documentation purposes. A property named 'secure' inside @metadata() carries no security semantics and does not mark the parameter as secure. Wrong: d. @secure() is not valid on int parameters, and changing the type would break the VM resource definition, which expects a password string. To pass numbers or arrays securely, you wrap them in a secureObject or serialize them as a secureString.

dominio: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources
sotto_argomento: Deploy resources by using an Azure Resource Manager template or a Bicep file
domanda: A Bicep file named main.bicep begins with the line targetScope = 'subscription' and declares a Microsoft.Resources/resourceGroups resource. You must deploy the file by using the Azure CLI. Which command should you run?
opzione_a: az deployment group create --resource-group RG1 --template-file main.bicep
opzione_b: az deployment sub create --location centralus --template-file main.bicep
opzione_d: az deployment mg create --location centralus --template-file main.bicep
spiegazione: Correct: b. A Bicep file whose targetScope is 'subscription' is deployed with az deployment sub create, and subscription-level deployments require a --location value. The deployment location is where the deployment metadata is stored and is separate from the location of the resources being deployed. Wrong: a. az deployment group create targets the resource group scope. It cannot deploy a file whose targetScope is 'subscription', and a resource group cannot be created from inside a resource group scoped deployment. Wrong: c. The command is the right one, but --location is mandatory for subscription-level deployments; omitting it makes the command fail. Wrong: d. az deployment mg create targets the management group scope and requires targetScope = 'managementGroup' in the file.

dominio: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources
domanda: Your main.bicep file sets targetScope = 'subscription'. You must extend it so that the resources defined in storage.bicep are created in an existing resource group named RG-Prod, which is in the same subscription. Which property must you add to the module declaration?
spiegazione: Correct: d. To deploy a module at a scope that differs from the parent file, set the module's scope property to a valid scope object. The resourceGroup() scope function returns that object for an existing resource group, so scope: resourceGroup('RG-Prod') deploys the module's resources into RG-Prod. Wrong: a. targetScope is a file-level statement that appears once at the top of a Bicep file; it is not a property of a module declaration. Wrong: b. Passing the resource group name as a parameter only supplies a string value to the module; it does not change the scope at which the nested deployment runs, so the resources would still target the subscription and the deployment would fail. Wrong: c. dependsOn only forces ordering between deployments; it has no effect on scope, and a scope function is not a valid dependency target.

dominio: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources
sotto_argomento: Deploy resources by using an Azure Resource Manager template or a Bicep file
domanda: During a clean-up project, an engineer maintains a Bicep file with targetScope = 'subscription' that assigns policies and creates resource groups. Obsolete policy assignments that were created outside the file still exist, and the engineer proposes running az deployment sub create with --mode Complete so that Resource Manager removes them. You must explain why this approach will not work and what to do instead. What should you tell the engineer?
opzione_a: Complete mode works at the subscription scope only after all resource locks in the subscription are removed.
opzione_b: Complete mode is supported only from the Azure portal, so the deployment must be re-run from the Template deployment blade.
opzione_c: Complete mode requires the what-if operation to be run first with --confirm-with-what-if; otherwise Resource Manager silently falls back to incremental mode.
opzione_d: Subscription-level deployments do not support complete mode; use deployment stacks to delete resources that are no longer defined.
spiegazione: Correct: d. Subscription level deployments do not support complete mode. Microsoft's guidance is that complete mode is being gradually deprecated and that deployment stacks are the supported way to perform resource deletions with Bicep files or ARM templates. Wrong: a. Locks are relevant to complete mode only at the resource group scope, where a locked resource group prevents complete mode from deleting resources. Removing locks does not make complete mode available at the subscription scope. Wrong: b. The reverse is true: the portal currently does not support complete mode, so it is not an alternative path. Wrong: c. What-if is strongly recommended before any complete mode deployment because it shows what will be deleted, but it is not a prerequisite, and Resource Manager never silently downgrades a requested mode.

dominio: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources
sotto_argomento: Export a deployment as an Azure Resource Manager template or convert an Azure Resource Manager template to a Bicep file
domanda: To reproduce a production environment in a test subscription, an administrator selects a resource group that contains a Windows virtual machine, chooses Export template in the Azure portal, and downloads the ARM JSON template with Include parameters selected. When the template is deployed to the test subscription, the deployment fails because the local administrator password required by the virtual machine is not defined anywhere in the template. What is the most likely cause, and how should the administrator resolve it?
opzione_a: Some password parameters can be missing from exported templates; the administrator must consult the template reference and add the missing parameters manually.
opzione_b: Include parameters was misused; clearing that option makes Resource Manager generate the password parameter automatically.
opzione_c: The password was exported as an encrypted secureString value, but it can only be decrypted in the source subscription.
opzione_d: The administrator should export the template from the resource group's deployment history instead, because that option includes the original password value.
spiegazione: Correct: a. Microsoft documents this explicitly as a limitation of the export feature: some password parameters might be missing from exported templates. You must check the template reference and manually add these parameters before the exported template can be used to deploy resources. Wrong: b. Include parameters controls whether the autogenerated template parameters are emitted at all; clearing it means you author your own parameters, so it removes parameters rather than adding a missing password parameter. Wrong: c. Azure never returns secure values through the export API. Secure parameter values are not saved to the deployment history and are not exported in any form, encrypted or otherwise. Wrong: d. Exporting from history returns an exact copy of the template that was used for the deployment, but secure parameter VALUES are still not stored in the deployment history, so this does not supply the password.

dominio: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources
sotto_argomento: Export a deployment as an Azure Resource Manager template or convert an Azure Resource Manager template to a Bicep file
domanda: Before adopting the Export template feature as part of your infrastructure-as-code migration, you must document its constraints for the team. Which of the following statements about exporting templates are true? Select all that apply. Each correct answer presents part of the solution.
opzione_a: Exporting a resource group that contains more than 200 resources fails with the error 'Export template is not supported for resource groups more than 200 resources'.
opzione_b: The export template feature does not support exporting Azure Data Factory resources.
opzione_c: Exporting from the deployment history returns an ARM JSON template only; it cannot produce a Bicep file directly.
opzione_d: Exported templates are guaranteed to be production ready and can be redeployed without modification.
opzione_e: The Azure CLI can export a resource group directly as a Bicep file by using az group export --output bicep.
spiegazione: Correct: a. Microsoft documents a limit of 200 resources for the resource group you create the exported template for, and returns exactly that error message when the limit is exceeded. Correct: b. The export template feature explicitly does not support exporting Azure Data Factory resources; you must instead use the copy or clone a data factory guidance. Correct: c. The Save from history option supports exporting only ARM JSON templates. To get Bicep from a historical deployment you export the JSON and then decompile it. Wrong: d. The opposite is documented: export is not guaranteed to succeed and is not a reliable way to turn pre-existing resources into production-usable templates. Most exported templates require adjustments before they can be deployed. Wrong: e. Bicep files can currently be exported only from the Azure portal. The Azure CLI and Azure PowerShell export ARM JSON, which you then pass to the decompile command.

dominio: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources
domanda: A colleague submits a pull request that adds several decorators to a Bicep file. You must approve only the usages that compile. Which decorator usages are valid? Select all that apply. Each correct answer presents part of the solution.
opzione_a: @secure() applied to a parameter of type object.
opzione_b: @maxValue(24) applied to a parameter of type string.
opzione_c: @minLength(1) applied to a parameter of type array.
opzione_d: @batchSize(2) applied to a module declaration that uses a for expression.
spiegazione: Correct: a. The @secure() decorator applies to parameters of type string and object, matching the secureString and secureObject types in ARM templates. Correct: c. @minLength and @maxLength apply to array and string parameters. For arrays the length is the number of items, so @minLength(1) on an array is valid. Correct: d. @batchSize is one of the two decorators available for modules (the other is description), and it can be applied only to a resource or module definition that uses a for expression. It makes the instances deploy serially in batches of the specified size. Wrong: b. @maxValue and @minValue apply only to int parameters. To constrain the length of a string you use @maxLength. This swap is the classic mistake. Wrong: e. The @allowed decorator is only permitted on param statements. To declare that a property must be one of a set of predefined values in a type or output statement, you use union type syntax instead.

dominio: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources
domanda:
You are hardening a Bicep file that deploys a storage platform. The file must meet the following requirements:
- The storageAccountName parameter must accept only values between 3 and 24 characters.
- The adminPassword parameter must never appear in the deployment history.
- The storage module, which is declared with a for expression, must deploy its instances two at a time instead of all at once.
- The environmentName parameter must accept only the values dev, test, or prod.

Select the correct decorator for each requirement.
opzione_a: Constrain storageAccountName to 3-24 characters: [@minLength(3) and @maxLength(24) | @minValue(3) and @maxValue(24) | @allowed([3, 24])]
opzione_b: Keep adminPassword out of the deployment history: [@secure() | @description() | @metadata()]
opzione_c: Deploy the module instances two at a time: [@batchSize(2) | @maxValue(2) | @sealed()]
opzione_d: Restrict environmentName to dev, test, or prod: [@allowed(['dev', 'test', 'prod']) | @discriminator('environmentName') | @sealed()]
spiegazione: Dropdown 1: @minLength and @maxLength set the minimum and maximum length for string and array parameters, and the values are inclusive. @minValue/@maxValue apply only to int parameters, and @allowed lists permitted values rather than a length range. Dropdown 2: @secure() marks the parameter as sensitive so that the value is not saved to the deployment history and is not logged. @description() only supplies help text, and @metadata() attaches arbitrary custom properties with no security effect. Dropdown 3: @batchSize(int) is applied to a resource or module definition that uses a for expression and deploys the instances serially in batches of the given size; the default is fully parallel. @maxValue constrains an int parameter, and @sealed applies to object types to elevate BCP089 from a warning to an error. Dropdown 4: @allowed takes an array of permitted values and the deployment fails validation if another value is passed. @discriminator is used for custom-tagged union data types, and @sealed relates to typo detection on user-defined types.

dominio: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources
sotto_argomento: Deploy resources by using an Azure Resource Manager template or a Bicep file
domanda: Contoso stores its infrastructure as Bicep files. An engineer must run several deployments from a workstation that has both the Azure CLI and Az PowerShell installed. Select the correct option for each requirement.
opzione_a: Cmdlet that deploys main.bicep when the file sets targetScope = 'subscription': [New-AzSubscriptionDeployment | New-AzResourceGroupDeployment | New-AzManagementGroupDeployment]
opzione_b: Azure CLI command that deploys main.bicep to an existing resource group: [az deployment group create | az deployment sub create | az group deployment create]
opzione_c: Switch that is mandatory for a subscription-scope deployment: [--location | --resource-group | --mode]
opzione_d: Deployment history name when main.bicep is deployed without specifying a deployment name: [main | A generated GUID | The name of the resource group]
spiegazione: Dropdown 1: To deploy at the subscription scope with Azure PowerShell you use New-AzSubscriptionDeployment, which is an alias of the New-AzDeployment cmdlet. New-AzResourceGroupDeployment targets the resource group scope and New-AzManagementGroupDeployment targets a management group. Dropdown 2: az deployment group create is the current command for resource group scope deployments. az deployment sub create targets the subscription scope, and az group deployment create is the retired command replaced by az deployment group create. Dropdown 3: Subscription, management group, and tenant deployments must all provide a location, because the deployment location determines where the deployment data is stored; it is separate from the location of the resources being deployed. --resource-group is not valid at the subscription scope, and --mode is optional and defaults to Incremental. Dropdown 4: If you do not provide a name for the deployment, its name becomes the name of the Bicep file, so deploying main.bicep produces a deployment named main. A GUID is generated for an unnamed MODULE (nested deployment), not for the top-level deployment.

dominio: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources
sotto_argomento: Export a deployment as an Azure Resource Manager template or convert an Azure Resource Manager template to a Bicep file
domanda:
Contoso has built its Azure estate manually over several years and now wants the existing configuration captured as Bicep files in a Git repository. An engineer investigates the export and decompile tooling and makes the following three claims. Evaluate each claim and indicate whether it is correct.

1. Selecting a deployment in the resource group's deployment history in the Azure portal and choosing Template lets you download the deployment as a Bicep file.
2. Running az group export --name RG1 > main.json and then az bicep decompile --file main.json produces a file named main.bicep.
3. Converting an ARM JSON template to Bicep and then building it back to JSON always reproduces the original JSON syntax exactly.
opzione_a: Selecting a deployment in the resource group's deployment history in the Azure portal and choosing Template lets you download the deployment as a Bicep file.
opzione_b: Running az group export --name RG1 > main.json and then az bicep decompile --file main.json produces a file named main.bicep.
opzione_c: Converting an ARM JSON template to Bicep and then building it back to JSON always reproduces the original JSON syntax exactly.
spiegazione: Statement 1 is No. The Save from history option supports exporting only ARM JSON templates. It retrieves an exact copy of the template used for that deployment, and you must decompile the JSON afterwards if you want Bicep. Bicep files can be exported only from a resource group or an individual resource, and only from the Azure portal. Statement 2 is Yes. This is the documented export-and-convert workflow: az group export writes the resource group's ARM JSON to main.json, and az bicep decompile --file main.json creates main.bicep in the same directory as main.json. Statement 3 is No. The decompile and build commands produce templates that are functionally equivalent, but they might not be identical in implementation. Converting a template from JSON to Bicep and back to JSON can produce a template with different syntax than the original, although the deployed result is the same.

dominio: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources
domanda:
A Bicep file named main.bicep begins with the line targetScope = 'subscription'. A developer is refactoring the file and proposes the following three changes. Evaluate each proposal and indicate whether the statement is correct.

1. You can declare a Microsoft.Resources/resourceGroups resource in main.bicep by using the resource keyword.
2. You can declare a Microsoft.Storage/storageAccounts resource in main.bicep by using the resource keyword and target it at a resource group by setting the scope property on that resource.
3. If you omit the name property from a module declaration in main.bicep, the file fails to compile.
opzione_a: You can declare a Microsoft.Resources/resourceGroups resource in main.bicep by using the resource keyword.
opzione_b: You can declare a Microsoft.Storage/storageAccounts resource in main.bicep by using the resource keyword and target it at a resource group by setting the scope property on that resource.
opzione_c: If you omit the name property from a module declaration in main.bicep, the file fails to compile.
spiegazione: Statement 1 is Yes. Microsoft.Resources/resourceGroups is one of the resource types supported at the subscription level, and creating resource groups is the canonical use of a subscription-scope Bicep file. Statement 2 is No. In a Bicep file, all resources declared with the resource keyword must be deployed at the same scope as the deployment. A storage account is a resource group scoped resource, so it cannot be declared directly in a subscription-scope file. To deploy resources at a different scope within the same deployment you add a module and set the module's scope property, which triggers a nested deployment. Note that this restriction does not apply to existing resources, which can be referenced at a different scope. Statement 3 is No. The name property of a module is optional. If no name is provided, a GUID is generated as the name for the nested deployment resource. Omitting the name is in fact a documented way to guarantee unique module names when the same module is deployed concurrently to the same scope.

dominio: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources
sotto_argomento: Export a deployment as an Azure Resource Manager template or convert an Azure Resource Manager template to a Bicep file
domanda: A resource group named RG1 was built entirely through the Azure portal. You must capture its current configuration as a Bicep file that your team can refine and commit to source control. You plan to use the Azure CLI and the Bicep CLI on your workstation. Which four actions should you perform in sequence?
opzione_b: Run az group export --name RG1 > main.json
opzione_c: Review the generated main.bicep, fix the reported warnings, and rename the autogenerated symbolic names
opzione_d: Run az login and select the target subscription by using az account set
spiegazione: Correct order: d, b, a, c. First you sign in with az login and, because the workstation has access to multiple subscriptions, select the correct one with az account set; otherwise az group export runs against the wrong context. Second, az group export --name RG1 > main.json writes the resource group's current state as an ARM JSON template, since the Azure CLI cannot export Bicep directly. Third, az bicep decompile --file main.json converts that JSON to main.bicep in the same directory. Fourth, you review the result: decompilation is a best-effort conversion with no guaranteed mapping from JSON to Bicep, so you might need to fix warnings and errors, and exported templates typically carry autogenerated symbolic names and variable names that should be renamed before the file is fit for reuse. The decompile step cannot precede the export step because main.json does not exist yet, and reviewing the Bicep file is only possible once it has been generated.

dominio: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources
sotto_argomento: Deploy resources by using an Azure Resource Manager template or a Bicep file
domanda: You have a Bicep file named storage.bicep that deploys a storage account. You must deploy it to a new resource group named RG-App in the East US region by using the Azure CLI, supply the parameter values from a Bicep parameters file, and confirm what the deployment will change before it runs. Which five actions should you perform in sequence?
opzione_a: Run az group create --name RG-App --location eastus
opzione_b: Run az login and set the subscription context by using az account set
opzione_c: Run az deployment group create --name AppDeploy --resource-group RG-App --parameters storage.bicepparam
opzione_d: Create storage.bicepparam containing a using './storage.bicep' statement and the parameter values
opzione_e: Run az deployment group what-if --resource-group RG-App --parameters storage.bicepparam
spiegazione: Correct order: b, a, d, e, c. You must first authenticate with az login and select the correct subscription with az account set. Next, because you are deploying to a resource group that does not exist, you create it with az group create; a resource group scope deployment cannot create its own target resource group. Then you author storage.bicepparam; the using statement inside the file points at storage.bicep and supplies the parameter values. You then run the what-if operation to preview the changes the file will make and to validate it for errors. Finally you run az deployment group create. Note that when you pass a .bicepparam file to --parameters, you must not also pass --template-file, because the using statement already identifies the template; supplying both raises the error 'Only a .bicep file is allowed with a .bicepparam file'. The same applies to the what-if command, which has identical permission and input requirements to the deployment command.
